opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came at a moment when I was asking myself what kind of impact I actually wanted my PhD to have. In the earlier years I was doing fairly standard research: you pick a problem, you write a paper, it gets accepted, and then, quite often, very few people actually use what you built. That started to feel a bit hollow to me.

When large language models took off, it became really clear that inference was going to be a huge bottleneck. Training gets all the headlines, but once a model exists, serving it efficiently to many users is where a lot of the real cost and engineering difficulty lives. vLLM was right at that point. It started from a research idea, PagedAttention, but it very quickly became infrastructure that people depended on every day.

So for me it fit on a few levels. First, I'd always been interested in the systems side: compilers, PyTorch internals, how things actually run on the hardware. vLLM let me work on exactly those problems, but with real constraints and real users instead of toy benchmarks. Second, open source gives you a very fast feedback loop. If you make something faster or break something, you hear about it within hours from people all over the world. That's a very different kind of validation from peer review, and I found it much more motivating.

And third, I think there was a bit of a bet involved. Many people would say spending a lot of PhD time on engineering-heavy open-source work is risky, because it doesn't map neatly onto paper counts. But I felt that in this era, building something that becomes a shared foundation for the community is itself a form of research contribution, maybe even a more durable one. Looking back, I don't regret that bet at all.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts conventional paper-focused research with building useful, real-world systems and says open-source work was more motivating. It does not clearly state that You prioritized hands-on systems-building experience over publishing machine-learning systems papers.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

Honestly, it wasn't a carefully planned decision at first. I was in the later stage of my PhD at Tsinghua, and I had already published the papers I needed. I'd done work on transfer learning, on PyTorch compilation, and I felt a bit stuck in a familiar rhythm: find a problem, run experiments, write a paper, submit, wait for reviews. The papers got accepted, but I kept asking myself how many people actually used what I built. Often the honest answer was very few.

Around the time ChatGPT came out, it became obvious to me that large models were going to change everything, and that the real bottleneck was shifting from training to inference. Everyone could see the models were powerful, but getting them to serve users cheaply and reliably was still very hard. When I started looking at vLLM, I realized this was a place where an engineering contribution could reach tens of thousands of developers almost immediately. If I fixed a bug or made the engine faster, people would feel it the next week. That kind of feedback loop was something academia had never given me.

There was also a personal reason. I had spent years becoming very familiar with PyTorch internals, with compilers, with distributed systems. Those skills were a bit scattered in my research, but in vLLM they all suddenly mattered at the same time. It felt like the project was designed for what I happened to know.

And for the PhD itself, I didn't see it as a distraction. My advisor was supportive, and I framed it this way: a PhD is supposed to train you to do something nobody has done before and to have real impact. Open source gave me a different path to the same goal. Instead of measuring myself by citations, I could measure by downloads, by the companies deploying it, by the people in the community who said this saved them. So joining vLLM wasn't leaving research. It was finding the version of research that actually fit who I wanted to be at that stage.

r001.rationale: The response favors impactful engineering work and open-source contributions over the academic paper cycle, but it does not clearly state that Kaichao prioritized gaining hands-on systems-building experience over publishing machine-learning systems papers.

astra-6.text: At that stage of my PhD, I wanted to work on problems where research and practical impact were closely connected. vLLM offered that combination: interesting systems challenges, but also a way to put ideas into software that people could actually use. It felt like an opportunity to go deeper on a research problem while learning from how it behaved in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says vLLM combined research with practical impact and usable software, but it does not state that Kaichao prioritized hands-on systems building over publishing machine-learning systems papers when changing research directions.

sol-6.1.text: At that stage of my PhD, I wanted to work on something that was technically interesting and useful in practice. vLLM felt like a good fit because it connected research on efficient inference with a system people could actually use. You could identify a bottleneck, work on it, and see the effect in real workloads. That combination of research questions and practical impact was what attracted me.
